intuition: Try all index triples in O(n^3) time, then deduplicate their sorted values. Sorting exposes monotonic choices and reduces the search to O(n^2). Repeated values make enumeration especially wasteful: many distinct position triples describe exactly the same three values.

Sorting gives pointer movement a direction. With anchor -1, a total below zero cannot be fixed by decreasing the right value, so only increasing left can help. A positive total requires decreasing right. This argument lets one comparison eliminate many pairs. Duplicates need separate treatment because a correct zero-sum pair might be followed by identical values at adjacent positions; skipping them preserves completeness while enforcing unique output triplets.

For a fixed first value, a sum below zero rules out every pair using that left value with a smaller right value. A sum above zero similarly rules out that right value with a larger left value. Therefore pointer movements cannot skip a solution. Distinct anchors and duplicate skipping emit each value triplet exactly once. Sorting uses a copied array; each anchor scans the remaining range once.

steps: Anchor -4 cannot reach zero: even the largest available pair gives -4+1+2=-1.
For anchor -1, pointer values -1 and 2 give the triple sum -1-1+2=0; record [-1,-1,2].
Move inward to 0 and 1; their total with -1 is zero, giving [-1,0,1].
Skip the next equal anchor -1; later anchors produce no additional distinct triplets.

codeNotes.note: The sorted copy creates monotonic order without requiring the original array to remain reordered.
A repeated anchor would re-enumerate the same value triplets, even though its position is different.

codeNotes.note: After a match, ignore equal left values so that the same triplet cannot be emitted again.
